'''Wendy Laurel Freedman''' {{post-nominals|country=GBR|FRS}} (born July 17, 1957) is a Canadian-American astronomer, best known for her measurement of the [[Hubble's law|Hubble constant]], and as director of the [[Carnegie Institution of Science|Carnegie Observatories]] in [[Pasadena, California]], and [[Las Campanas Observatory|Las Campanas, Chile]]. She is now the John & Marion Sullivan University Professor of Astronomy and Astrophysics at the [[University of Chicago]].<ref name="uchicagonews">{{cite web|last1=Koppes|first1=Steve|title=Wendy Freedman, world-leading astronomer, joins UChicago faculty|url=http://news.uchicago.edu/article/2014/08/07/wendy-freedman-world-leading-astronomer-joins-uchicago-faculty|website=UChicago News|accessdate=8 July 2017|language=en|date=7 August 2014}}</ref> Her principal research interests are in [[observational cosmology]], focusing on measuring both the current and past expansion rates of the universe, and on understanding if there is missing physics in the standard (Lambda Cold Dark Matter) cosmological model.

In 2025, ''[[Time (magazine)|Time]]'' magazine listed her as one of [[Time 100|the world's 100 most influential people]].<ref>{{Cite magazine |date=2025-04-16 |title=Adam Scott: The 100 Most Influential People of 2025 |url=https://time.com/collections/100-most-influential-people-2025/7273826/adam-scott/ |access-date=2025-04-16 |magazine=TIME |language=en}}</ref>

==Early life and career==
Freedman grew up in Toronto<ref> Maureen Searcy, [https://mag.uchicago.edu/science-medicine/cosmic-cuisine Cosmic cuisine], ''The University of Chicago Magazine'', 110,4 (December 21, 2016).</ref> in a Jewish family,<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.aip.org/history-programs/niels-bohr-library/oral-histories/46903 | title=Wendy Freedman }}</ref> the daughter of a medical doctor and a concert pianist.<ref name="nutt">Amy Ellis Nutt, "[http://www.nj.com/specialprojects/index.ssf?/specialprojects/index.ssf?/specialprojects/seekers/seekers5.html Will the universe disappear, or does a mysterious force have other plans for it?] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304034030/http://www.nj.com/specialprojects/index.ssf?%2Fspecialprojects%2Findex.ssf%3F%2Fspecialprojects%2Fseekers%2Fseekers5.html |date=2016-03-04 }}" The Star-Ledger, Newark, NJ (December 5, 2002)</ref> Her early interest in science was kindled by a formative high-school physics class. This led her to the [[University of Toronto]], where she was first a [[biophysics]] student, then an astronomy major, receiving her B.Sc. in 1979.<ref name="nas">National Academy of Sciences, "[https://web.archive.org/web/20150905215708/http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/podcasts/interviews/wendy-l-freedman.html InterViews: Wendy L. Freedman]"</ref> She remained at Toronto for her graduate work, receiving a Ph.D. in astronomy and astrophysics in 1984.<ref name="ciw">Carnegie Institution, "[http://obs.carnegiescience.edu/users/wendy The Carnegie Observatories: Director] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120531012531/http://obs.carnegiescience.edu/users/wendy |date=2012-05-31 }}"</ref> Joining the Carnegie Observatories in Pasadena, California, as a post-doctoral fellow in 1984, she became a faculty member of the scientific staff three years later as the first woman to join Carnegie's permanent staff. In 2003 she was named to the Crawford H. Greenewalt Chair and Director of Carnegie Observatories.<ref name="ency">Elizabeth H. Oakes, Encyclopedia of World Scientists, "[https://books.google.com/books?id=uPRB-OED1bcC&dq=Wendy+Freedman+1957&pg=PA251 Wendy Freedman]"</ref> Freedman's early work was principally on the [[Cepheid variable|Cepheid distance scale]] and the stellar populations of nearby galaxies.

==Hubble constant==
Freedman was co-leader of an international team of 30 astronomers to carry out the [[Hubble Space Telescope]] Key Project, a program aiming to establish the distance scale of the Universe and measure the current expansion rate, a quantity known as the [[Hubble constant]]. This quantity determines the size of the visible universe and is key to determining its age. Over the course of the Key Project, the team measured the distances to 24 galaxies using [[Cepheid variable]] stars, and measured the Hubble constant using five independent methods. The project's researchers, led by Freedman, published their final result in 2001.<ref name="nas" /><ref>{{Citation | last1 = Freedman | first1 = W. L. | last2 = Madore | first2 = B. F. | title = Final Results from the Hubble Space Telescope Key Project to Measure the Hubble Constant | year = 2001 | journal = Astrophysical Journal | volume = 553 | issue = 1 | pages = 47–72| arxiv = astro-ph/0012376 | bibcode = 2001ApJ...553...47F | display-authors=1 | doi=10.1086/320638| s2cid = 119097691 }}</ref> The work provided a value of the Hubble constant accurate to 10%, resolving a long-standing, factor-of-two debate.

She continues to refine her measurements of the Hubble constant using not just Cepheid variables but also the method of the [[tip of the red-giant branch]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Freedman |first=Wendy L. |date=2021-09-01 |title=Measurements of the Hubble Constant: Tensions in Perspective* |journal=The Astrophysical Journal |volume=919 |issue=1 |pages=16 |arxiv=2106.15656 |bibcode=2021ApJ...919...16F |doi=10.3847/1538-4357/ac0e95 |issn=0004-637X |s2cid=235683396 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Giant Magellan Telescope==
Freedman initiated the [[Giant Magellan Telescope]] (GMT) Project and served as chair of the board of directors from its inception in 2003 until 2015. GMT is an international consortium of leading universities and science institutions to build a 25-meter optical telescope at the [[Carnegie Institution for Science]]'s [[Las Campanas Observatory]] in the Chilean Andes. With a primary mirror {{convert|80|ft|m|abbr=off|sp=us}} in diameter, the GMT is poised to be the world's second largest ground-based telescope when it is completed. The telescope, which has entered its construction phase and is expected to become fully operational by 2034, will be able to produce images 10 times sharper than those of the Hubble Space Telescope.

==Recognition==
[[File:Dr. Wendy Freedman and U.S. Ambassador to Chile, Paul Simons.jpg|thumb|Freedman with the American ambassador to Chile in 2009]]

Freedman has been elected a member of the US [[National Academy of Sciences]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/podcasts/interviews/wendy-l-freedman.html?referrer=https://www.google.com/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304085109/http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/podcasts/interviews/wendy-l-freedman.html?referrer=https://www.google.com/|url-status=dead|archive-date=March 4, 2016|title=Wendy L. Freedman|website=www.nasonline.org}}</ref> the [[American Philosophical Society]],<ref>{{Cite web|title=APS Member History|url=https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?creator=Wendy+Freedman&title=&subject=&subdiv=&mem=&year=&year-max=&dead=&keyword=&smode=advanced|access-date=2021-05-14|website=search.amphilsoc.org}}</ref> the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]],<ref name="AAAS Arts">{{cite web | title=Wendy Laurel Freedman | website=American Academy of Arts & Sciences | date=5 January 2025 | url=https://www.amacad.org/person/wendy-laurel-freedman | access-date=6 January 2025}}</ref> and a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]]<ref name="uchicagonews"/> and a Legacy Fellow of the American Astronomical Society. She was elected [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] in 2023.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Wendy Freedman |url=https://royalsociety.org/people/wendy-freedman-36213/ |access-date=2023-05-24 |website=royalsociety.org}}</ref>

She has received several awards for her contributions to observational cosmology, including a Centennial Lectureship of the American Physical Society (1999), the John P. McGovern Award in Science (2000),<ref name="ency" /> the [[Magellanic Premium|Magellanic Premium Award]] of the [[American Philosophical Society]] (2002)<ref>Sigma Xi, "[http://www.americanscientist.org/authors/detail/wendy-freedman American Scientist On-Line: Wendy Freedman]"</ref> and the [[Marc Aaronson Memorial Lectureship|Marc Aaronson Lectureship]] and prize (1994) "in recognition of a decade of fundamental contributions to the areas of the extra galactic distance scale and the stellar populations of galaxies".<ref>{{cite web|last1=Thompson|first1=David J.|title=Measurement of Cosmological Parameters - Wendy Freedman|url=https://scicolloq.gsfc.nasa.gov/Freedman_2016.html|website=Goddard Scientific Colloquium|publisher=NASA Goddard Space Flight Center|accessdate=8 July 2017|date=9 March 2016}}</ref> In 2009 Freedman was one of three co-recipients of the [[Gruber Cosmology Prize]].<ref>{{Cite web|title = Wendy L. Freedman {{!}} The Gruber Foundation|url = http://gruber.yale.edu/cosmology/2009/wendy-l-freedman|website = gruber.yale.edu|access-date = 2016-01-28}}</ref> She received the 2016 [[Dannie Heineman Prize for Astrophysics]],<ref>{{Cite web|title = Dannie Heineman Prize for Astrophysics {{!}} American Astronomical Society|url = https://aas.org/about/grants-and-prizes/dannie-heineman-prize-astrophysics|website = aas.org|access-date = 2016-01-28|archive-date = 2016-01-21|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160121053552/http://aas.org/about/grants-and-prizes/dannie-heineman-prize-astrophysics|url-status = dead}}</ref> awarded jointly by the [[American Institute of Physics]] and the [[American Astronomical Society]], "for her outstanding contributions and leadership role in using optical and infrared space- and ground-based observations of Cepheid stars, together with innovative analysis techniques, to greatly improve the accuracy of the cosmic distance scale and thereby constrain fundamental cosmological parameters."<ref>{{cite web|last1=Koppes|first1=Steve|title=Wendy Freedman to receive Heineman Prize for Astrophysics|url=https://news.uchicago.edu/article/2016/01/20/wendy-freedman-receive-heineman-prize-astrophysics|website=UChicago News|accessdate=8 July 2017|language=en|date=20 January 2016}}</ref>

She was elected a Legacy Fellow of the [[American Astronomical Society]] in 2020 <ref> {{cite web|url=https://aas.org/grants-and-prizes/aas-fellows|title=AAS Fellows|publisher=AAS|accessdate=27 September 2020}} </ref>

In 2024, she was included in [[Nature's 10|''Nature''<nowiki/>'s 10]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Nature's 10: the people who helped shape science in 2024 |url=https://www.nature.com/immersive/d41586-024-03890-5/index.html |access-date=2024-12-19 |website=www.nature.com |language=en}}</ref>

In 2025, Freedman was a recipient of the [[National Medal of Science]].<ref name="National Medal of Science">{{cite web | author=The White House | title=President Biden Honors Nation's Leading Scientists, Technologists, and Innovators | website=The White House | date=3 January 2025 | url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2025/01/03/president-biden-honors-nations-leading-scientists-technologists-and-innovators/ | access-date=4 January 2025}}</ref>

In 2026, Freedman received a Doctor of Science degree from [[Clark University|Clark University]].

Asteroid [[107638 Wendyfreedman]], discovered by [[David Healy (astronomer)|David Healy]] at the [[Junk Bond Observatory]] in 2001, was named in her honor.<ref name="MPC-object" /> The official {{MoMP|107638|naming citation}} was published by the [[Minor Planet Center]] on 6 January 2007 ({{small|[[Minor Planet Circulars|M.P.C.]] 58597}}).<ref name="MPC-Circulars-Archive" />

==Personal life==
Freedman is married to longtime collaborator Barry F. Madore. They have two children.<ref name="nutt" /><ref>Corbis Images, [http://www.corbisimages.com/stock-photo/rights-managed/RR005239/galactic-astronomers Galactic Astronomers]"</ref>
